Its Core Ultra 9 285H and 32GB of DDR5 RAM can easily handle demanding productivity, content creation, and heavy multitasking. The integrated NPU acceleration also makes AI workloads run efficiently. Plus, the 1TB SSD provides plenty of storage. It’s pricey for a mini PC, but the premium hardware makes it a very capable compact workstation on a discount. Mini PC deals FAQ 1. What should you look for when buying a mini PC? The first thing you have to check off your list is just what configuration you need to get your job done. Are you going to use your new mini PC for browsing only? Then a cheap budget-friendly device with a decent CPU and 16GB of RAM will do the trick. Do you want it to be able to juggle a bunch of apps and not choke on 50 browser tabs? Then a more powerful CPU and at least 32GB of RAM would be better. Do you want to do some light gaming in your downtime? Look for a device that comes with a GPU or Occulink connectivity to hook up an external GPU instead. Are you looking to utilize the mini PC as a home server? Your priority then should be a large SSD—2TB or more. There are devices for each and every one of these scenarios, and they’re all quite affordable. The best part is that mini PCs are… well, small, so they can be placed practically anywhere depending on your intended use and available space. They also support multiple monitors out of the box, which makes it easy to replace your old, larger desktop and you won’t even need to pay for extra hubs. 2. Can a mini PC replace a desktop computer? For most people, the answer is “yes”! Mini PCs are definitely powerful enough to replace desktops for most users, especially if you’re going to use it for work, browsing, or streaming movies. If you want something for photo and video editing, or even gaming, there are models that allow you to do that, but they’ll cost a bit more. If you’re into hardcore gaming, however, you’re still better off with a proper gaming PC or laptop. 3. Can a mini PC run modern games? Mostly, yes. But it will ultimately depend upon the mini PC you buy and which modern games you want to play. Some high-performance mini PCs can run modern AAA games. You might not be able to run them at the highest settings though, and performance will depend heavily on the specific hardware. If you do want to game on a mini PC, look for powerful models with dedicated discrete GPUs such as an Nvidia RTX or AMD Radeon rather than integrated graphics. Alternatively, you can opt for cloud streaming services to game on less powerful mini PCs, which bypasses the need for high-end hardware. 4. Which mini PC brands are reliable? Some of the most reliable mini PC brands are Minisforum, Beelink, GMKtec, and Geekom. Of course Apple’s Mac minis are also excellent computers if you prefer using macOS. Brands such as Asus, Lenovo, HP, and Dell all make high-quality smaller-footprint PCs, but they might not fill the same niche and/or they are typically more expensive.

item.title: What does Amazon know about you? The answer is buried in your account info
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
We all know companies profile us. But understanding that abstractly is one thing. Reading the words “has flat buttocks” in your Amazon account is very much another. If you’re not on Threads, this discovery is one of the latest viral posts . A woman stumbled upon this assumption while in her Amazon settings, buried among other, less inflammatory ones within the Your Shopping preferences section. Of course, having read that post myself while doomscrolling before bed, I resolved to look at my own profile in the morning. (I have a vested interested in privacy as a topic, after all.) Turns out, Amazon has little incendiary commentary about me. You might even say I’m boring. Here’s how you look it up. On a desktop PC, head to Account . Under Ordering and shopping preferences , click on Your shopping preferences . Then look for Manage your information at the bottom of the page. You should then see a page titled About You , listing details that Amazon says it uses to “personalize your experience for you and everyone you shop for.” Amazon / PCWorld For me, Amazon believes I like technology and photography. And I prefer Command strips for mounting hardware. That’s about it. As you might guess, these assumptions are based on your shopping habits—and surprisingly upfront. (Finding the equivalent information on Facebook feels like a labyrinth of clicks, and the details aren’t as blunt as “has flat buttocks.”) As disappointed as I am Amazon’s spiciest commentary on me was “prefers white networking cables,” I got a good lesson from looking up my profile. One, it confirms that where and how you shop affects the data that businesses collect. Two, it’s a good reminder that I should keep looking up these details on different websites and services. And three, this will only get more complicated as agentic AI services pull in and collate data about us through friends, family, and associates.

item.title: The Surface Laptop Ultra is an AI monster with a laptop problem
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Microsoft’s new Surface Laptop Ultra is powered by a Mediatek CPU and Nvidia’s powerful RTX Spark SoC, which is mainly designed to run local AI models on the user’s lap. Five competing laptops—from Dell, HP, MSI and more—will offer additional options. Here’s the thinking. Microsoft is banking on near-future AI developers and enthusiasts running local AI models and tools directly from their PC. If needed, they’ll tap Microsoft’s Copilot AI for more horsepower. Microsoft calls this “hybrid intelligence” and it’s basically an acknowledgement that users won’t necessarily care which device does what. It’s a compromise, as is most anything that’s AI-related in productivity: some love it, others despise it. There are further tradeoffs. Users will be able to run models locally, but the Surface Laptop Ultra ships with a 140W power adapter. That’s a signal that it will consume much more power than typical laptops, though not gaming laptops. (That’s another question: is this a gaming laptop? Microsoft showed just a single Gears of War game running on the Ultra, with no indication of frame rate.) Nevertheless, I left the Windows and Surface Event with a question that no one at Microsoft could answer: What will be the battery life of these laptops? In one demonstration, Microsoft employee Kayla Cinnamon proudly put the Surface Laptop Ultra into “airplane mode,” showing how the laptop could run entirely disconnected from a network. (Microsoft’s official stance: “Battery life details for Surface Laptop Ultra will be shared closer to availability,” reads the Ultra’s spec page . “It varies based on usage, settings, configuration, and other factors.”) But these laptops may not even work on airplanes. For one, 140W is more than some airplane power outlets can supply—110W to 150W is apparently typical. (Edit: Jason Rabinowitz, cohost of the AVTalk podcast and an avid airline enthusiast, says that 60 to 100 watts is actually more common.) Will you be able to run AI agents continuously throughout a 13-hour flight from San Francisco to Taiwan? I very much doubt it. We don’t even have a reliable way to test the battery life while churning tokens. All of these unknowns left the analysts I spoke to shaking their heads. Who’s going to buy these devices? The $2,599 price is the base, which means as users scale up to more and more memory—to run larger and more powerful AI models—the price will balloon with it. We’re still in 2026, a time when the $699 Apple MacBook Neo blew up headlines. “I think it’s very obvious that no one wants to spend all this crazy money [on cloud AI],” said analyst Bob O’Donnell, principal at Technalysis. But how users want to divvy up their work between slower local AI and faster, more expensive cloud models remains to be seen. It seems we have a new breed of laptops that might not really be laptops at all—they may not have the battery to last with how much power they chug, and they can’t plug in while on the go. They’re “portable” AI workstations for a niche of users who are willing to pay more than what it costs for a normal productivity laptop, for “productivity” loathed by some of its users. Whew. Updated at 2:02 PM with additional detail.

Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ): Further considerations Plugable’s dock means that you can connect to three 4K displays, even if you don’t absolutely have to. Read our full Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI and DisplayPort Display Horizontal Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ) review Other USB-C hub/dock reviews and features Anker Nano 13-in-1 USB-C dock review: This combo USB-C dock/hub doesn’t deliver the amount of charging power I’d hope for, though the two-for-one special is unique. Mokin 160W GaN All-in-One Station : With great power comes great…performance. Ugreen’s $5 cable deal: Deals come and go, but check back for an attractive price. USB-C buying guide : Our friends at PCWelt have some advice on how to differentiate USB from Thunderbolt. How we test USB-C hubs We test USB-C hubs/dongles slightly differently than docking stations. A separate article offers a detailed explanation on how we test USB-C hubs , but here’s a short summary: First we test the physical configuration, and how ports are spaced and whether filling one port impedes use of the port next to it. We also run performance tests to make sure ports function as advertised. Finally, we consider price and weight it against functionality and build quality. More complex hubs usually command more money, but that’s not always the case! Who curated this article? My name is Mark Hachman , and I’ve been working as a technology reporter and reviewer for 30 years. I review USB-C hubs/dongles, Thunderbolt docking stations, and DisplayLink docks, so I have a good handle on the different types of I/O technologies being used and what will be best for you. I’ve been reviewing these devices since work-from-home became popular in 2020, realizing pretty quickly that home users wanted a mix of displays and legacy peripherals. How to choose the best USB-C hub You’ll want to do a careful of assessment of your work equipment and your needs in order to find the right hub or dock for yourself. First, take stock of your peripherals Here’s where to start: Take a look at the peripherals you own, or plan to buy. Do you have an old external hard drive that uses a traditional USB-A cable? Do you manually back up photos from an SLR camera via its SD card? Or is your Wi-Fi connection unreliable enough that you’d prefer Ethernet? Figure out what ports you’ll need. This advice is for Windows users; Macs have their own limitations on USB-C connections. Keep in mind that you may want to use both a mouse and keyboard, and possibly connect a printer, too. You can disconnect a keyboard to print, but it’s kind of a pain. Even if you own a modern 2026 laptop, you may still have hardware from several years ago. A hub bridges your laptop to its peripherals, but can serve as a bridge to the past, too. This laptop has several USB-C ports, but if yours has just one, you’ll want to daisy-chain the laptop’s power cord by plugging it directly into the hub, like so. Next, check out what ports your laptop already has It’s also important to take stock of your laptop or tablet’s ports: Does it have one USB-C port or two? If your device only has one port, is there a separate charging connection? If your laptop or tablet has a USB-C port and uses it exclusively for charging , you’ll want to buy a USB-C hub with a dedicated charging input port. Note how much input power the port allows, and confirm that it will be sufficient for your laptop. Otherwise, you’ll be forced to choose between charging your laptop and accessing other devices, which makes little sense. Most laptops will pop up a warning about a “slow charger” if your laptop’s not getting enough juice. A laptop’s USB-C port. Matt Smith/IDG Video adds another wrinkle. Older laptops often included dedicated video ports, often HDMI; modern laptops in 2026 may include a dedicated video port as well. But video can also run over the USB-C port through a technology called DP Alt Mode which enables certain USB-C ports to send video signals to external monitors using the DisplayPort protocol, via the USB-C cable. The problem, even as manufacturers like BenQ admit , is that these cables aren’t often properly labeled. There’s no way for us to tell you whether your USB-C port can support video passing over it. You’ll need to consult your laptop’s manual to tell. If the port does support video, you can either use a USB-C hub to connect to an external monitor. Alternatively, you can run the USB-C cable to a display with a USB-C cable input. These USB-C displays have only been available for a few years, but they provide an alternate way of routing video out of your laptop. Assess your laptop and peripheral power needs Desktop hubs will often take power in from an external charger like the one you plug into your phone, and use it to power your laptop. On these hubs or dongles, there will be a dedicated USB-C input port to accept power, but not data. A powered laptop docking station, on the other hand, ships with its own charger — which may be hardwired into the docking station and take will power in and also push it out to peripherals. As I noted above, the input power to your laptop needs to be sufficient to power it. But if you’re investing in a powered USB-C docking station, check our reviews to see how much power the hub or docking station can push out to peripherals. The 2026 iPhone 17 Max consumes 40W of charging power to fast-charge the phone; most docking stations won’t get near that. But an older phone, such as an Apple iPhone 14, only needed 30W of charging power. Older phones need even less power to fast-charge them. You certainly don’t have to buy a USB-C docking station or hub to charge a phone; most hubs weren’t built with them in mind. It’s useful to know, however, what your hub or docking station will be able to do or not do. Making sense of the USB-C technologies A USB-C port on your laptop can either run at 5Gbps or 10Gbps, with the latter being almost ubiquitous these days. That’s plenty of bandwidth for a printer, a mouse, a keyboard, or a hard drive, even all at once. Products like displays, Ethernet, and high-speed SSDs gobble up that bandwidth, however. Display technologies tend to have the most influence over what you should buy. If you simply want to connect to an external 1080p display — or two — a USB-C dongle should work fine, provided that the dongle has the available ports. It’s certainly the cheapest option. If you want to connect more displays with higher resolution, you may have to examine other choices. Traditionally, the only other alternative was a Thunderbolt dock . Provided your laptop had a Thunderbolt port, Thunderbolt’s 40Gbps bandwidth allows for two 4K displays, running at 60Hz, plus various peripherals. (You can use a 10Gbps USB-C dock even if you have a 40Gbps Thunderbolt port, but only 10Gbps of that throughput will be available to the 10Gbps dock.) Thunderbolt is usually associated with laptops which use Intel processors; laptops with AMD Ryzen or Qualcomm Snapdragon chips inside use the “generic” equivalent, also called USB4. There are also two intermediary technologies to choose from: a DisplayLink USB-C dock, and a USB-C dock that takes advantage of something called HBR3 and DSC. DisplayLink , owned by Synaptics, uses software compression between your laptop and the dock to approximate a Thunderbolt experience over a generic USB-C connection. It requires a software driver, but our experience is that it’s an excellent choice for office work, but not gaming. Here are the best DisplayLink docks and why to buy them. HBR3 with Display Compression ( HBR3 with DSC ) is essentially an industry standard version of DisplayLink. The problem? The technology hasn’t been widely publicized, let alone supported. Our experience has been that docks that support HBR3 work well with laptops using 12th-gen Core processors on up. Laptops with a 10th-gen Core chip inside them aren’t supported, and 11th-gen Core laptops are iffy. If you own a laptop chip with a 12th-gen Core chip or one that’s even more recent, you stand a good chance of success. Otherwise, don’t bother. Thunderbolt cables and ports include the little lightning-bolt icon, which differentiates them from the otherwise unmarked USB-C cables. Finally, don’t worry about platform branding Because USB-C is common among Macs, Windows PCs, and phones, some hubs align their branding with a particular platform. Go ahead and use that USB-C that’s billed as being “for MacBook Pro, Chromebook, and XPS” with any Windows PC — we did, and it works just fine. You won’t need any special software or drivers. After testing our USB-C hubs, we can confirm that some no-names perform just as well as their more well-known counterparts, and for less money, too. One thing to keep in mind: Because price is so critical to our recommendations, know that some of the prices may change as manufacturers offer sales. Therefore some hubs we didn’t recommend primarily based on price could become more purchase-worthy. FAQ 1. Why buy a USB-C hub or dongle? Remember when laptops used to contain all sorts of ports: USB-A, HDMI, SD card slots, and more? And do you remember how svelte the early Macintosh laptops looked, especially when Apple began removing all of the ports in favor of USB-C and Thunderbolt? PC makers did, and decided that was the approach that they would take, too. Unfortunately, that left laptop owners like you with the problem of legacy hardware: printers, keyboards, SD card, micro SD cards, and so on — and with no ports to plug them into. Enter the USB-C hub, an inexpensive product that helps solve that problem. Just pay attention to what ports the USB-C hub offers, to make sure it meets your needs. 2. I don’t understand what the difference is between a USB-C hub, a DisplayLink dock, and a Thunderbolt docking station. What do I need? Here’s the short answer: If you want to connect your laptop to a printer, an SD card or microSD card, mouse, keyboard, or legacy 1080p monitor, stick with a basic 10Gbps USB-C hub/dongle. If you want to add a pair of additional displays (especially 4K), or high-speed SSD drives, we’d recommend you look at our list of 40Gbps Thunderbolt docking stations . Generally, the larger, powered docks offer more features. It is confusing, since they all use the “same” USB-C port. Generally, most modern laptops have a small Thunderbolt “lightning bolt” logo to help distinguish the faster port. 3. What’s the difference between a USB-C hub, USB-C dongle, and a USB-C docking station? A USB-C hub or dongle (we use the terms interchangeably) is a small, portable device that you can slide into a bag or backpack. A USB-C docking station tends to be heavy and bulky enough that you’ll want to keep it on your desk. It’s not true that a USB-C docking station will have more features than a USB-C hub, as some compact USB-C hubs pack in a surprising number of ports. Docking stations tend to be bigger and bulkier, and are designed to live on your desk. If there’s anything that docking stations tend to have that dongles sometimes don’t, it’s a USB-C port designed only to accept power from your laptop’s USB-C charger. That allows you to gain additional ports as well as charging capabilities from the same dock. 4. How much does a USB-C hub or dongle cost? Expect to pay between $30 and $40 for a good USB-C hub, even in 2026 — maybe a bit more with tariffs. USB-C docking stations are bigger and bulkier but add even more capabilities. We’d expect you to pay over $100 for these. 5. How much does price matter when buying a USB-C hub or dongle? Honestly, not much. Pay attention to our reviews and those from other shoppers, but buy according to what the hub or dongle offers. You can absolutely find solid USB-C hubs and dongles for an inexpensive price. USB-C docking stations , though, can feel a bit overpriced. In part, that’s because Thunderbolt docks were wildly expensive during the 2020 to 2021 pandemic years. USB-C docking stations are an alternative, but their prices were nudged upward, too. Fortunately, prices have come down, as the supply chain regained a semblance of normalcy. 6. What is the difference between USB-C and Thunderbolt? Both USB-C and Thunderbolt use the same USB-C connection. The difference is that a “generic” USB-C connection typically provides 10Gbps of bandwidth, and Thunderbolt provides 40Gbps, or 120Gbps with Thunderbolt 5 . Thunderbolt ports are becoming much more common, so it’s possible that your laptop won’t have any “USB-C” ports; they’ll be Thunderbolt-enabled instead. (To tell the difference, consult your laptop’s manual or look for a small “lightning bolt” logo over the port itself. That’s usually a sign that it’s a Thunderbolt port.) A USB-C dongle and a Thunderbolt dock are similar, in that they both provide a number of additional ports. There’s a key difference, though. The rule of thumb is that a USB-C dongle provides enough bandwidth for two 1080p displays at 60Hz, or a single 4K display at 30Hz. (Staring at any 30Hz display for a length of time can tire out your eyes, so I don’t recommend it.) A Thunderbolt dock, however, allows enough bandwidth to connect two 4K displays at 60Hz, plus all the peripherals you wish to attach. If you don’t need big, high-resolution displays, don’t buy a Thunderbolt dock and purchase a USB-C hub instead. 7. What’s a DisplayLink USB-C dock? A DisplayLink USB-C dock is what you might call a “tweener” device: something between USB-C and Thunderbolt. DisplayLink docks embed a small chip from Synaptics in the docking station, and require use of a software driver that you’ll need to download. (USB-C and Thunderbolt are essentially plug and play.) The Synaptics chip compresses the data, and gives you the ability to connect (no joke) up to three or sometimes four 4K display all over a 10Gbps USB-C cable. It feels a bit like black magic. They’re not foolproof; DisplayLink docks are best for office work (email, Word, Excel, and so on that don’t require a whole lot of bandwidth, because the images are largely static) and web browsing. Transfer a lot of data (or play back a lot of high-bitrate video) and you’ll see some stuttering. We used to break out DisplayLink docks into their own page, but we now include recommendations on this list of the best USB-C hubs, as well as our list of the best Thunderbolt docks . If you shop smart, you can get the capabilities of a Thunderbolt dock, for less. 8. Can you connect a USB-C dongle to a Thunderbolt dock? Or to another USB-C hub? You can absolutely connect a USB-C hub to a Thunderbolt dock. You probably won’t be able to connect a USB-C dongle to another USB-C dongle/hub, but if your laptop has more than one USB-C port, you can connect a USB-C hub to each. Thunderbolt offers the ability to “daisy-chain” devices, however, so you can connect one Thunderbolt dock to another. USB-C, however, does not. 9. Why do USB-C hubs get so hot? USB-C hubs can get warm or even hot while using them to transfer data or charge devices. This is because the electronic components and circuitry within hubs build up heat during use. Depending upon the hub’s material, heat can become trapped inside the hub leading it to become hot to the touch. If you are concerned about your hub becoming too hot during use, you may consider purchasing a hub made from metallic parts, such as aluminum, so that heat can more easily dissipate as it builds up. Even though two USB-C hubs may have wildly different brand names, you may sometimes find that they’re otherwise identical or just very similar. We’ve given you a lot of detail on what makes a good USB-C hub or dongle and what to consider when buying one. In general, however, these are fairly inexpensive, flexible ways to upgrade your laptop, and I’d recommend always carrying one in your laptop bag!

item.title: Still on Windows 11 24H2? You have one week to upgrade
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
If you’re still on Windows 11 24H2, time is running out. Microsoft is ending support for that version of Windows this month, so you’ll need to upgrade to either 25H2 or (ideally) 26H2 as soon as possible. If you don’t, you’ll put your system at increasing risk over time. Support for Windows 11 24H2 ends on October 13th, 2026 —less than a week from today. Once that deadline hits, you’ll no longer receive security, feature, or quality-of-life updates on your PC. How do you know if you’re still on 24H2? You can check by opening Windows Settings (use the Windows key + I keyboard shortcut), clicking “System” in the left panel, scrolling all the way down to “About” in the right panel, scrolling down to the “Windows specifications” section, and spotting what it says for “Version.” If you’re on 24H2, it’ll say “24H2.” (Also make note of “Edition,” which will likely be “Windows 11 Home” or “Windows 11 Pro.”) Microsoft explicitly states on this support page : Windows 11, version 24H2 Home and Pro editions will reach end of updates on October 13, 2026. Devices running these editions will no longer receive fixes for known issues, time zone updates, technical support, or monthly security and preview updates containing protections from the latest security threats. Enterprise and Education editions remain supported until October 12, 2027. In other words, the end of support will only affect PCs running Windows 11 Home or Pro editions. Windows 11 Enterprise and Education editions will get another year of support, ending on October 12th, 2027. This extra year is in line with Microsoft’s standard practice and isn’t specific to 24H2. Windows 11 26H2 is already available , so you should upgrade to that if you can. To do so, open Windows Settings again and navigate to “Windows Update” in the left panel, then enable the “Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available” option in the right panel. Then, wait until the Windows Update page shows “Windows 11, version 26H2 is available.” Even though the update has a few known issues for some users , it has some important optimizations that speed up Windows 11 performance on older hardware , so it’s worth taking the leap. That’s one of the areas in which Microsoft is indeed improving Windows 11. item.title: Building a PC in 2026 is all about choosing your compromises
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Anyone who wants or needs a new desktop computer has long had a choice to make: Buy a ready-built computer or build one yourself from individual components. The choice isn’t always that simple, and there are several factors that can make either option appealing. The price of a pre-built computer always includes, in one way or another, the cost of assembling it. If you build it yourself, you can spend all your money on getting the best possible components and pay for the assembly with your own time and by taking on the risk yourself. Build your own computer. Anere Lusina But building your own computer also offers incredible freedom and a sense of pride in what you can achieve yourself. It’s something that’s difficult to quantify in terms of money, but for many people, that’s the biggest draw. What does it mean to build a computer yourself? If you’ve never attempted to build a computer before, it can feel like a big and daunting task. But just like putting together an Ikea kitchen, it’s something the vast majority of people can manage if they just take the time and do their research. And unlike a kitchen, you don’t need to worry about any potential water leaks — at least, not unless you decide to build a system with water cooling! Building a computer basically involves three separate tasks: planning and buying components; fitting the components into the case; and configuring the BIOS, installing the operating system, and testing that everything works as it should. The first is the most complex, as there are so many components to choose from. Fortunately, you don’t need to learn and keep track of everything yourself, as there are plenty of websites with computer-building tools that help you put together components that are compatible with one another. Assembling the components isn’t actually that complicated, but you should definitely read a guide or two and watch a few YouTube videos that walk you through the whole process step by step. With video guides, for example, you can see how cable routing works in practice and pick up lots of little tips that make the build easier and safer. The same goes for learning about the BIOS and how to install Windows — familiarize yourself with these process before you begin. Advantages of building your own PC Total flexibility – you choose all the components. It can be very satisfying to use a computer you’ve built yourself. It’s usually cheaper. Plenty of scope for upgrading later. Disadvantages of building your own computer Choosing components is complicated and can take a lot of time. You take the risk that something might go wrong during the build. Advantages of buying a ready-built computer You get a ready-built computer without any risk or effort. You can find computers on sale, which can lower the overall price. Disadvantages of a pre-built computer It’s unlikely you’ll find a computer with exactly the combination of components you’d prefer. Many pre-built computers have an older processor, slightly slower memory, or some other compromise. What should I do if something goes wrong or breaks? It’s a good idea to order components so that they all arrive at the same time and you can assemble the computer within the standard return window. If any component were to malfunction, you could easily return and replace it without the hassle of making a warranty complaint. Should any component break later on, you can either contact the manufacturer or the seller for recourse under the product’s warranty. Cable management is an important but not particularly glamorous part of building a computer. Andrey Matveev Still, it is, of course, your own responsibility to assemble the computer safely. This means, among other things, that you must avoid discharging static electricity, but also ensure that components are fitted correctly. Some graphics cards are so heavy that they may need to be braced to avoid damaging the PCI Express slot, so read and follow all instructions carefully, both for the components and the case you have chosen. Computer builders A middle ground between buying a ready-built computer in a shop and building one yourself is to have a PC custom built by a vendor. For instance, boutique PC vendors such as iBuypower and Cyberpower will build a PC to your specification, taking care of the assembly and testing. But you’ll need to buy all the components from them, which of course doesn’t always give you the best price or choice. How to find your way through the component jungle If you enjoy getting deep into the details, you can, of course, take it upon yourself to keep track of all the components and ensure that the ones you choose are compatible with one another. However, most people choose to use a computer-building tool. The site PC Part Picker is the best known of these. With these tools, you can, for example, start with a specific case, a specific motherboard, or a specific graphics card. Once you have selected a component, the lists of other components are filtered to show only those that are compatible with your first choice, and the process continues in this way. If you try to select something that is not compatible with one of the other components you have chosen, you will receive a warning. Compatibility has two aspects: technical and physical. The technical aspect concerns, for example, whether a memory module fits a particular motherboard, or whether that motherboard supports a particular processor. A compact computer is more complicated to build and to select the right components for. Đào Hiếu In terms of size, it is simply a question of whether the components will fit inside the chosen chassis alongside the other selected components. Does the processor cooler protrude high enough above the memory modules to avoid interference when you choose high-performance memory with large built-in coolers? Will the long graphics card fit into the space inside the chassis? With a generously sized chassis and an ATX or E-ATX motherboard, you can usually fit almost anything in, but it’s still worth double-checking. And if you want to build a more compact computer in a small chassis with a Mini-ITX motherboard, the dimensions suddenly become very important. Which components are most important, and where can I cut corners? This depends on what you’ll be using the computer for, how you view future expansion options, and your sense of aesthetics. The graphics card is a key component, especially for gamers. Rafael Pol Graphics card If you’re looking to play high-end games with high graphics settings, the graphics card is undoubtedly the most important component, and you can cut corners on almost everything else to make room in your budget for it. If you can afford it, you’ll benefit greatly from choosing an AMD processor with so-called 3D V-Cache (indicated by ‘x3D’ at the end of the model name), such as the previous-generation Ryzen 5 7500X3D. The expanded cache means that gaming performance is less dependent on the speed of the main memory, so you can cut back there — something that can save you a fair bit of money given today’s memory prices. For anyone interested in running local AI, the graphics card is also important, but in this case it is primarily the amount of graphics memory that matters. And for AI, you can easily combine two cheaper graphics cards instead of one more expensive one, which isn’t possible for gaming. Be careful when inserting the processor into its socket. IT Services EU Processor For everyone else, the processor and graphics card are roughly equally important. My suggestion is that you choose one of the latest models, as they tend to be more efficient, feature the latest technologies, and will be fully supported by Windows for longer. Something to consider is whether you want to buy a processor and graphics card at roughly the same level, or opt for a slightly more powerful one and a slightly simpler one, with the aim of upgrading the latter at a later date. By opting for a cheaper graphics card, you can get a new, more powerful one in a couple of years’ time, while still benefiting from the slightly better processor you chose from the start. Memory and storage Most people won’t notice any practical difference between a blazing-fast SSD with PCIe 5.0 and a cheaper one with PCIe 4.0. When it comes to storage, a reliable manufacturer and a model that has received good reviews are more important than maximum speed, and you can save a fair bit by skipping the cutting-edge technology. When it comes to memory, capacity is the most important factor. Really fast memory is only important for a few specific use cases and is never worth it for the average user. If you’re using Windows, 16GB is the minimum you’ll need. Given today’s prices, it’s understandable if you want to save as much as possible on memory. Unless you know you’ll be running a great many programs simultaneously, or individual memory-intensive programs such as virtualized operating systems or Adobe Photoshop, 16GB should be enough. As long as your motherboard has four memory slots, you can always buy more later. Other components The case is something many people choose to skimp on, but this often means the computer looks less stylish and, perhaps more importantly, is more fiddly to build. Furthermore, it may have poorer airflow and, consequently, poorer heat dissipation, resulting in higher temperatures and lower performance. I would therefore recommend that you at least look at review ratings and choose a chassis that suits your needs, even if it costs a bit more. Another important component is the power supply unit; here, you need to ensure that its capacity is high enough for the components you’ve chosen, as well as any future upgrades you think you might need. Efficiency and noise levels are other factors worth bearing in mind. The power supply is important. Don’t skimp, but don’t go overboard either. Andrey Matveev For other components, you can often get by with cheaper models, but I recommend sticking to trusted brands and reading reviews. For example, there are some really good, inexpensive CPU coolers, but also a few real duds. These recommendations obviously apply even if you choose to buy a pre-built computer — don’t just focus on the processor, graphics card, and memory; check the case, power supply, and other components as well. What initially seems like a bargain can soon turn into an expensive lesson if you have to upgrade several components. Don’t forget future expandability When comparing a pre-built computer — whether it’s a traditional tower model with standard components, a mini-PC or something more exotic — with one you build yourself, you shouldn’t overlook the possibilities for expanding and upgrading the computer in the future. If you build it yourself, for example, you can choose two larger memory modules instead of four smaller ones. It’ll be more expensive now, but you can buy more later. In most pre-built systems, all the memory slots are filled, unless you buy a very small amount of memory. A mini-PC rarely has more than two slots, and many have soldered-on memory that can neither be expanded nor replaced with larger modules. Upgrade your computer with more memory, storage, or a new processor. Andrey Matveev Storage can almost always be replaced, but in tower models and home-built machines there are usually empty M.2 slots that you can fill without having to replace the existing storage. With a traditional tower computer, there may be spare PCI Express slots that you can use for additional storage, new network cards or other components you may later realise you need. This applies whether you buy a ready-built system or build it yourself, but the number of slots available varies greatly from one motherboard to another. Ten years ago, it was common to have several spare slots, but nowadays many manufacturers choose to focus on more M.2 slots for SSDs, and sometimes there’s only one extra slot apart from the one intended for the graphics card. Or not even that. Compare the total cost Corner. Andre Tan If you’re mainly looking to get as much computer as possible for your money, I suggest you look at both pre-built computers and the various components you’ve selected. Don’t forget to add a Windows licence if you need one, and any peripherals such as a monitor, mouse, and keyboard. Then compare the total price. item.title: Windows Search is becoming your PC’s new AI-powered control center
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
For years — decades, really — the entry point inside Windows has been the Start menu. But from what Microsoft showed as part of its AI vision for Windows 11 this week, Start might be on its way out. Instead, Windows Search may be the app you connect with first when you want to get things done. Yes, Windows Search, the humble search box buried in your taskbar and at the top of the Start menu. Microsoft plans to embed even more functions inside it, including Actions, essentially mini-widgets for controlling features like Windows’ dark mode. Think of it like a chat box already built into your PC, and you can start to see where this is going. Eventually, Windows Search will start calling on other applications, including Copilot, to provide answers and complete tasks. Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Windows, says “thousands” of these actions are headed your way by year’s end. You’re not just searching. You’re doing. Weird. Or is it? Let’s back up a bit. In July, Microsoft said it was moving to a quieter, purpose-built iteration of Windows Search , following an earlier mega-memo about simplifying and focusing Windows. That included cutting out unnecessary uses of Copilot — bye, Notepad Copilot — and moving to a new framework called WinUI 3, which Microsoft thinks is more efficient and will speed up Windows as a whole. Old and new: to the right is where Windows Search is now . Read on for its next evolution. That’s happening, Microsoft said this week, as part of an update provided to Microsoft’s Experimental Insider Channel. Windows is getting faster! That’s good. But from a design standpoint, things are getting a little odd. Originally, the Search app featured recommended content, highlighting offbeat holidays like World Otter Day and suggesting games to play. That was too unfocused, so the July update pared back the recommended content. The update also polished features such as detailed document previews, making it easier to make sure you had the right file. Previews will return to Windows Search this fall, but in a new format. However, Microsoft’s upcoming Search update concluded that not enough people were clicking on the previews — were they supposed to? — so those rather nice-looking previews are disappearing, too. For now, anyway. Later this year, Windows Search will add those document and web page previews back as small cards in the list of Search results, along with “widgets” like weather and stock price, plus visual results for queries like “How tall is the Eiffel Tower?” Too rich? Not rich enough? Microsoft can’t seem to make up its mind. Windows chief Pavan Davuluri explains Microsoft’s new AI vision within Windows. Mark Hachman / Foundry What “hybrid intelligence” means to you This isn’t about two design teams squaring off in the cafeteria over variable fonts, though. There’s a reason. Windows Search is responsible for turning up the right document and information both on the user’s PC and online, and that dichotomy is the tricky balance Microsoft is carefully navigating. Wednesday’s official launch of the Surface Book Ultra and competing third-party devices ushered in what Microsoft calls “hybrid intelligence,” a way of balancing intelligence based in the cloud (Bing, Copilot) with information stored and searched for on the PC (File Explorer). Nvidia’s RTX Spark superchip (tied to a Mediatek Arm CPU) is being asked to run AI locally on the PC. Well, some AI, anyway — Microsoft wants to balance how cloud and local AI interact. It just so happens that Windows Search is one of the first places where this battle is being fought. In addition to the cards or widgets that Windows Search plans to add, there will be Actions, which Microsoft began talking about last year : turn on dark mode, adjust your mic volume, or turn on “do not disturb.” You can take a screenshot or adjust your windows positions, too. All of these capabilities have seeped into Windows over time, from the short-lived effort to have Copilot control your PC to adjustments made in the search bar within Windows 11’s Settings. Heck, Windows 10’s Cortana even allowed some of these changes. Cortana allowed you to send texts! Now Windows 11 will, too. Mark Hachman / Foundry “You can make these changes as fast as you can type,” Davuluri said. Copilot: less of an app, more of an ingredient That seems like a signal. Windows Search feels more like an iteration of Copilot than it ever has, where users type in what they want and Windows responds. That’s not far-fetched! Microsoft wants Copilot to “know” what’s on your PC, just as it wants it to know what you’re working on. It’s not that far from Microsoft understanding that the “Contoso spreadsheet” refers to a specific file to wondering if you want to book that same hotel in Maui you visited last year. (And it’s still a little scary.) Jacob Andreou, the executive tasked to lead the Copilot experience at Microsoft, showed Copilot with a big toggle switch next to “Hybrid Intelligence,” implying you’ll be able to flip it off if you want. Of course, the idea is that you won’t. Do you trust Microsoft to leave in the toggle switch? “Copilot now has access to three new things,” Andreou said. “First, local context. Local context means that Copilot can now [access] all of the local files on your PC… Second, local actions. Local actions means that Copilot can now take action directly on my machine. It can move files, it can change a setting, it has the same level of the ability to control and change things that I do as a user, but always with permission.” Copilot will also use the cloud when needed for complex tasks, but where “cost and privacy matter more, it can delegate down to local models that run directly on your computer,” Andreou added. Last month, Microsoft detailed a major update to Copilot , which would let you vibe-code Windows apps (Code) and design and set loose agents (Autopilot) on your PC. Andreou showed off how Autopilot could respond to a task from an accountant, assembling a bunch of tax documents. In the demo, Autopilot searched the user’s inbox, assembled the documents from OneDrive, the Documents folder, and other locations, collected them into a folder, renamed the files (?!) and then even bundled them into a zipped archive. Copilot then authored a email response and waited for approval. Renaming files, zipping files…Copilot will have control. “Copilot now truly understands your PC,” Andreou said, adding that this is Copilot “natively designed for Windows.” These new features will arrive in the next couple of months, he said. Is the future of PC work just giving orders? At one time, you typed in an address into a web browser. You visited Google to search. Today, every browser in existence allows you to search right from the URL bar and a similar transition feels like it’s occurring on the PC. Did I mention that you’ll be able to access Copilot from Windows Search, too? Microsoft has promised features like putting your PC into dark mode for years. And yet, time and again, it hasn’t quite delivered. It feels like Microsoft wants PC computing to be less about moving windows around with a mouse and more about telling your PC what to do. I mean, you’ll even be able to install LLMs when you set up a new PC. I’m sure that there will be more than one way to perform all these tasks, such as launching the Copilot app directly. But Microsoft wants to take its new AI-powered Windows and build a front door. And, well, who would have thought? That door is apparently Windows Search.

item.title: I used Claude to find the online accounts I’d forgotten about
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
When you’ve reviewed as many tech products as I have, you wind up with dozens of abandoned online accounts, most of them created and forgotten the moment I was done with my testing. Over the years, I’d started to wonder: How many of those accounts are still floating around, idle but still active? Good question, and I’m sure I’m not the only one curious about the online accounts they’ve left behind. A good method for tracking down forgotten online accounts is to scour your inbox for signup confirmations, and Consumer Reports has a detailed explainer on how to do just that. But I was curious to take it a step further, enlisting Claude’s help for a prompt that would automate the process, sifting through my email for me to catalog the accounts I’d collected over the years. This prompt takes two of Consumer Reports’s best ideas — searching through your email, as well as checking sites like haveibeenowned.com for possible account breaches — and hands the busywork to Claude Cowork or another AI agent, like Google’s Gemini Spark , Meta’s Muse , or a ChatGPT Dot . Now, this prompt does involve giving your agent access to your email, typically via a Gmail integration or connector (and all the four AI agents I just mentioned have one). If that prospect makes you uncomfortable — and that’s a perfectly reasonable reaction — by all means, skip this prompt. Still here? OK, here’s the prompt we’re going to use: Search my email from the last 5 years for signs that I created an account somewhere — welcome emails, “verify your email” or “confirm your account” messages, and password-reset emails. Build a new spreadsheet (a Google Sheet if you can) with one row per service: service name, website, date of the earliest signup email, date of the most recent email from them, and whether the service appears on haveibeenpwned.com’s public list of breached websites (with the breach year). For each service, find its official account-deletion page and add the link; if you can’t find one, write “not found” — don’t guess. Put services I haven’t heard from in 2+ years at the top. Don’t sign in anywhere, request password resets, type my email address into any website, delete anything, or contact anyone. This is a lengthy prompt, by design; rather than trying to prompt to alter an AI’s behavior, we’re telling the agent what we want it to do — and what not to do. Namely, this is a passive, hands-off search, meaning the agent won’t try to log onto any outside websites or ping anyone about your accounts. That also goes for the haveibeenowned.com search, with the agent only checking whether a given service has recently been compromised rather than plugging in your particular email address. When you’re done, you’ll get a spreadsheet that details all the online accounts the agent found, with the ones that appear the most dormant at the top. I tried this prompt with all four of the biggest consumer-level AI agents, and they all spat out their spreadsheets within anywhere from five minutes to half an hour. Each agent tagged at least 50 accounts, with my ChatGPT Dot leading the pack with 73 accounts detected. Looking over the spreadsheets, many of the discovered accounts are ones I recognized and use frequently: Facebook, Netflix, Hulu, Instagram, Microsoft, and Disney+ are all there, along with SeatGeek, Roborock, and OpenTable. But there were also some surprises and “oh, right”-type finds. I’d forgotten all about the Bowers & Wilkins account I’d signed up for way back in 2022 (I must have been reviewing a pair of B&W headphones), as well as a Hawaii Pacific Health MyChart account from 2023 (created, as I now recall, after I’d broken my toe during a Honolulu vacation). I also spotted a Dunkin’ Rewards account I have no memory of signing up for, along with Dick’s Sporting Goods (huh?), Golf Galaxy (no clue), and strangest of all, LocalFlirt (which, as it turns out, was one of those random “confirm your account” emails that slipped past my Gmail spam filter). The spreadsheets also include links for deleting the various accounts, although roughly half of them came back with “not found” or simply point to privacy FAQs. You’ll also see which of the various services have suffered recent breaches, although again, those notes don’t pertain to your specific email address. In any event, this “find my old accounts” prompt is a good example of the kind of busywork AI agents are good at, and I’ll be teeing up more for you in the weeks ahead.

item.title: Is the new Fire TV Stick 4K really faster? It depends
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Last week, Amazon launched a new Fire TV Stick 4K with a bold claim: It’s nearly 20 to 40 percent faster, the company says , than “a similarly priced 4K streaming stick from another leading brand.” Amazon won’t name the competitor, but in my own tests, the advantage over comparably priced streamers isn’t so clear-cut. What I tested Amazon’s own comparison video is impossible to test because it doesn’t show real-world results. Instead, it’s just a mock-up “for illustrative purposes,” based on Amazon’s measurements of “time from content selection to playback” in “the three most popular apps.” In addition to not naming the rival streamer, Amazon won’t say which apps it tested. So I decided to conduct my own measurements instead, looking at how long a few similarly priced streamers take to boot up, wake from standby, and start streaming. I also measured their ability to quickly switch between different apps. For these tests, I pitted the new Fire TV Stick 4K against Walmart’s Onn 4K Plus and Roku’s Streaming Stick Plus . Both Amazon’s and Roku’s sticks cost $60 and are often on sale for less. Walmart’s device is a small box rather than a streaming dongle, but it has a cheaper regular price of $50. (Walmart also sells a less-powerful dongle for $40 , but that’s not a fair comparison unless Amazon lowers the Fire TV Stick 4K’s retail price.) Boot times Here’s how long it takes to fully load each streaming device’s home screen after unplugging it and plugging it back in again. Fire TV Stick 4K: 23 seconds Onn 4K Plus: 33 seconds Roku Streaming Stick Plus: 22 seconds Roku has a slight edge here, though in most cases it won’t matter. If your device is plugged into an outlet, or your TV’s USB port supplies power when it’s off, rebooting will be a rare occurrence. (That said, it’s too bad Amazon’s and Roku’s streamers no longer ship with wall chargers or lengthy USB cables. If you want to plug them into an outlet — for instance, because your TV’s eco mode disables USB power when it’s off — you’ll have to bring your own charger.) Launching Netflix For this test, I waited until each streaming device’s home screen was fully rendered, then timed how long it took to load Netflix and start playing a video: Fire TV Stick 4K: 32 seconds Onn 4K Plus: 43 seconds Roku Streaming Stick Plus: 39 seconds I also ran a second test, waiting an extra 30 seconds before jumping into Netflix. This gave each device more time to fully boot: Fire TV Stick 4K: 15 seconds Onn 4K Plus: 23 seconds Roku Streaming Stick Plus: 19 seconds The Fire TV Stick 4K was the clear winner on both cases, validating Amazon’s claim of being 20 to 40 percent faster than the competition at least when Netflix is involved. Launching Apple TV While testing, I noticed that Netflix was launching faster from boot-up than other apps. To rule out any potential special treatment, I decided to run the same tests as above with the Apple TV app: Fire TV Stick 4K: 30 seconds Onn 4K Plus: 33 seconds Roku Streaming Stick Plus: 29 seconds And here are the results with a 30-second wait after booting: Fire TV Stick 4K: 25 seconds Onn 4K Plus: 24 seconds Roku Streaming Stick Plus: 27 seconds Interestingly enough, the Fire TV Stick 4K loses its advantage here, though the results are pretty similar across all three devices. Fast app switching The only thing better than an app that loads quickly is one that loads instantly. To that end, I tested how many apps you can switch between before any of them required a full reload: Fire TV Stick 4K: 3 apps Onn 4K Plus: 5 apps Roku Streaming Stick Plus: 4 apps The Onn 4K Plus has 2GB of RAM, versus 1GB on the other streamers, so it’s no surprise that Walmart’s box can keep more apps in memory. While its boot times are slower, it can feel faster as a result. Waking from standby Both the Fire TV Stick 4K and Onn 4K Plus enter sleep mode after 15 to 20 minutes of inactivity, while Roku streamers just show a screensaver indefinitely. Here’s how long each of them took to get back to their home screens: Fire TV Stick 4K: 5 seconds Onn 4K Plus: 2 seconds Roku Streaming Stick Plus: 2 seconds While Amazon’s Fire TV Stick 4K is a few seconds slower, you’ll probably end up waiting longer for your TV to power on anyway. Looking beyond load times Jared Newman / Foundry While it’s fun to measure these things and deflate Amazon’s marketing, ultimately a few seconds’ difference in load times won’t make or break the experience. What really matters is how easy it is to find what you’re looking for in the first place. On that front, the new Fire TV Stick 4K is similar to Amazon’s other streamers, with the same major home screen redesign that started rolling out earlier this year. It looks and behaves similarly to the Google TV software on Walmart’s Onn devices, but of course with more emphasis on Amazon Prime content. It’s also running Amazon’s new Vega operating system, which has more limited app support and does not allow sideloaded apps. The new system is more for Amazon than for you , but it’s also inevitable as Amazon says it won’t make any new streaming devices based on its old Android-based platform. All of which means that if you’re okay with the Fire TV experience, the new Fire TV Stick 4K could be a nice upgrade. Just don’t expect it to help you get where you’re going much faster. item.title: The smartest PC upgrade in 2026 isn’t a new computer — it’s a monitor
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
You’ve heard all of the stories about skyrocketing laptop and PC component costs. You’re trying to limit your tech expenses. Is there any way you can improve your workstation in 2026 that’s not completely going to bust your budget? There is. The one upgrade that you can and should make without hesitation right now your monitor — or monitors . A 27-inch 4K monitor can now cost less than many individual PC upgrades. You’ve probably heard this argument before: invest in something you’ll use for hours at a time. At night, you should sleep for (hopefully!) eight hours on a comfortable, supportive mattress. During the workday, you constantly touch a keyboard, but you’re always viewing the fruits of your labors on a display or two in front of you. Though some people might still work from just a laptop, I’m betting that the 2020 pandemic prompted you to set up a home office with at least a single external display. Let’s dig into why it’s time to upgrade your monitor. Welcome to PCWorld’s newsletter, Smart Mode! The focus of this newsletter is productivity: from software to hardware to peripherals, all with the idea to get what you need to get done, efficiently. I’m your host, Mark Hachman, covering the productivity tips, tools, and trends that you need to know about, both from within PCWorld and beyond. If you want the latest issue in your inbox each week, just sign up right here . Big is better You may have heard that more displays equal more productivity; larger displays do, too. A study (funded by NEC) found that 20-inch monitors returned an 18 percent improvement in performing tasks than an 18-inch monitor. If you own a Thunderbolt dock, you’re often best served by adding more displays. Is this overkill? Satechi And that makes sense, given that a 27-inch 16:9 display has about 3.5 times the display area of a 14-inch 16:10 laptop screen. You can simply see more. Likewise, an 18-study meta-review in 2021 also found that users uniformly preferred using at least two displays, and there was moderate evidence that they reduced desktop interactions, improving efficiency. So there’s evidence that buying more, larger displays works. A display with a 60Hz refresh rate is standard, but a higher refresh rate is easier on your eyes — if you can afford one, I think they’re worth it. My workspace includes a pair of Acer 4K 160Hz (XV275K P3) 27-inch displays (provided by Acer) that I use for testing the 4K capabilities of Thunderbolt 5 docks. They’re excellent for testing the high-end capabilities of I/O hardware, but they’re absolutely overkill for the average home office. Even two 27-inch displays can take up a great deal of desk space, which is why I rotate one into a vertical or portrait mode. New features for the same price?! So there’s an argument to be made for buying an upgraded display just on the numbers alone…but there’s more to it than just that. In 2024, IDC found that the average price of a display actually decreased. That was the result of “normal” market forces. Then 2025 arrived, and…display prices were hit again? Absolutely. Because the price of memory and storage skyrocketed, display prices benefited — laptop makers were desperate to find some place to save a buck, and displays were the answer. Panel makers pushed prices down. Obviously rising memory costs overshadowed that, at least for notebooks. However, the cost of IPS panels (and IPS displays) remained relatively flat, according to reports. Meanwhile, OLED displays entered the picture. In 2023, laptop makers like Samsung started building in self-emissive OLED displays into laptops like the Galaxy Book 3 Pro 360 , amazing everyone (me included) with their high-contrast displays, making video content pop. Quickly, however, they began adding the features IPS display buyers had become used to: higher and higher refresh rates, plus a greater number and diversity of I/O options, such as USB-C/Thunderbolt I/O. Don’t worry about going too big. A monitor arm or even the ability to rotate the display into portrait mode can save desk space while still preserving the benefits of a large monitor. Pexels Ideally, given what I’ve just recommended (about 27 inches, 4K, 60Hz refresh rate or better) we would simply add OLED to the mix to create what’s approaching (at least for me!) the perfect productivity monitor. We’re not quite there yet, unfortunately. While 4K, high-refresh-rate OLED displays exist, they’re typically considered to be gaming monitors like this Samsung 32-inch Odyssey OLED G7 ($749.99 at Amazon, 32% off at press time). Great display! I’d love to have it! But it’s still a little rich for my blood. Instead, if you’re willing to drop down a notch, consider this 27-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED or this Acer Predator 26.5-inch 240Hz OLED for $314.99. Both are 1440p displays, rather than true 4K, so there’s an unfortunate compromise. Still, doesn’t that seem a lot more affordable than a new PC? In my opinion, monitor prices have not only held steady throughout the past year or two, but they’ve shown continual improvement by adding new features and technologies. Something tech-related that’s improved while holding prices constant? Is that actually possible in 2026? So what should you buy? Remember, monitors typically fall into one or two categories: gaming and office productivity. I would recommend that you review our recent recommendations for productivity displays to see if in any deals are in effect. We list the current prices, so you’ll be able to check for deals. If you’re seeing this the day I published it, my colleague Michael Crider recently saw a 27-inch, 240Hz OLED gaming monitor on sale for $300 at Best Buy, at 1440p resolution. Snag it if it’s still there! Productivity in the news Speaking of OLEDs, how about a review of Samsung’s recent 4K Odyssey OLED monitor , too? Michael Crider has an app suggestion that straddles productivity and personalization: Wallpaper Engine . Here’s a quick way to test your Internet speed — right from your taskbar? Two websites one tab : it’s Firefox getting creative, again. Productivity on camera Remember my earlier newsletter in managing OneDrive? This is a more opinionated take . Much more. AI transcription is awesome, but expensive. Microsoft Word (yes, Word!) can save you money . Productivity tip for the week: AI is such a controversial subject these days, and I generally avoid it in favor of my own knowledge and expertise. But AI tools are certainly tempting, especially for cutting out some of the busy work. Cal Newport reminds me of this report from The Wall Street Journal earlier this year, where using AI tools required constant supervision — and supervision meant a loss of focus. That’s something for both you and me to think about, I think. Feel free to drop me a line on Bluesky or Twitter/X if you have any ideas. Thanks for reading! Thanks for tuning in to this edition of Smart Mode, PCWorld’s newsletter devoted to helping you make the most of your life, smartly. Sign up and have it sent to your inbox every Thursday!

item.title: Chuwi UniBook review: A $449 laptop that gets a lot right
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros Lightweight and sturdy aluminium casing Very long battery life Plenty of ports, including Gigabit LAN Comfortable typing experience and backlit keys Quiet and efficient cooling Cons Only 8 GB of soldered-on RAM Dull display Low CPU and graphics performance Our Verdict The Chuwi UniBook is a well-built, portable laptop with good battery life and connectivity. That said, its 8GB of RAM and mediocre display hold it back. Price at time of review This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Price Today Best Prices Today: Chuwi UniBook Retailer Price Chuwi $449 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide With the UniBook, Chuwi is introducing Intel’s affordable Wildcat Lake platform. At $449, the 14-inch laptop focuses on practicality rather than raw performance. Its key strengths are its lightweight form factor and wide selection of ports. The 8GB of RAM, however, raises questions about how it handles multitasking and more demanding tasks. Christoph Hoffmann Chuwi UniBook: Design and build quality The dark grey UniBook has an understated look and feels significantly more substantial than its price would suggest. The lid, keyboard bezel, and underside are made from an anodized aluminum alloy. The matte surfaces show fingerprints only some fingerprints. Our test unit is neatly assembled. We found no sharp edges, uneven gaps, or creaking joints. The lid bends slightly in the middle, but remains stable during normal use. Even the keyboard yields only a little under firm pressure. Measuring 12.38 × 8.70 × 0.65 inches, the UniBook takes up barely more space than a sheet of A4 paper. Chuwi states its weight as 2.65 pounds. This makes it significantly more portable than the MSI Modern 15, which, at 14.13 × 9.49 × 0.79 inches and 3.86 pounds, takes up more space in your bag. The compact 65-watt USB-C power adaptor also fits in well with the portable design. Christoph Hoffmann The hinge holds the screen securely in place and allows for an opening angle of 180 degrees. However, the base is too light to open with one hand. Christoph Hoffmann The backlit chiclet keyboard makes good use of the width of the chassis. The keys offer a clear actuation point and sufficient travel for longer texts. Two brightness levels make typing in dark environments easier. The backlighting shines through noticeably at the edges of the keys in places. Our test unit also features a US QWERTY layout without dedicated keys for umlauts and the ß. Prospective buyers should therefore check which keyboard layout the laptop comes with before purchasing. Due to the 14-inch format, there is no numeric keypad. The arrow keys are on the small side, but the rest of the layout remains clear and uncluttered. Christoph Hoffmann The touchpad measures approximately 12 × 7 centimeters. Its smooth surface responds precisely to movements. Clicks work across almost the entire surface, though they feel firmer at the top edge. The matt 14-inch screen has a resolution of 1920×1200 pixels in the practical 16:10 aspect ratio. This provides more vertical space for documents than a standard Full HD panel. Text appears sharp, whilst IPS technology ensures consistent viewing angles. The refresh rate is 60 hertz. This is sufficient for Office and video streaming. However, photos look noticeably washed-out and color-accurate editing is out of the question. Outdoors, there is a lack of brightness reserve. Christoph Hoffmann The matt finish is a welcome feature, as it reduces distracting reflections. The display does not flicker. However, with dark images, the backlight shines through slightly at the edges. Overall, Chuwi delivers impressive build quality. However, the UniBook does not match the torsional rigidity and build quality of more expensive premium devices. Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200 is pre-installed. Chuwi has omitted unnecessary additional programs, so the system appears tidy once set up. Christoph Hoffmann On our test unit, not all Intel components were correctly configured after the Windows setup. We had to install the available chipset, graphics and NPU drivers separately. Some of these are found by the Intel Driver and Support Assistant . Christoph Hoffmann Microsoft Office Professional Plus 2024 is already pre-installed. The package includes Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. An additional Microsoft 365 subscription is not required to use it. Christoph Hoffmann Chuwi UniBook: Webcam, microphone, biometrics The 722p webcam produces soft images with little detail. It’s adequate for occasional video conferences, but not for high-quality recordings. A mechanical slider covers the camera when required. An integrated microphone is also available for voice calls. T he stereo speakers are loud enough, but the sound is thin and lacking in bass. Headphones are recommended for films and music. Christoph Hoffmann Biometric login is not possible. The UniBook has neither a fingerprint sensor nor an infrared camera for Windows Hello. To unlock the device, you must use a PIN, password, or an external security key. Chuwi UniBook: Connectivity In terms of ports, the UniBook outperforms many of its competitors. On the left-hand side are two USB-C ports with USB 3.2 Gen 1, DisplayPort output, and Power Delivery. There’s also an HDMI 1.4b port and a USB-A port with 5 Gbit/s. Christoph Hoffmann On the right-hand side, we find two further USB-A ports (one of which supports USB 2.0 only), a micro-SD card reader, Gigabit LAN, and a 3.5-millimetre jack. Both USB-C ports can charge the laptop and power a 4K display at 60 Hertz via HDMI. A maximum of 4K at 30 Hertz is possible. Christoph Hoffmann The Realtek RTL8852BE module supports Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.2. High data transfer rates are possible on compatible Wi-Fi networks, though Wi-Fi 6E is not supported. The wired Realtek interface delivers 1 Gbit/s. The fold-out network port is a nice feature, especially if you work from home. Chuwi UniBook: Performance The UniBook is powered by Intel’s Core 3 304 from the Wildcat Lake series. The 15-watt chip combines a fast performance core with four energy-efficient cores, as well as five threads. The maximum clock speed is 4.3 GHz, and the L3 cache is 6 MB. The processor is manufactured using the Intel 18A process. The architecture is modern, but the limited expansion options place tight constraints on performance. Christoph Hoffmann In PCMark 10 , the laptop scored 4,917 points. The sub-scores of 7,765 points for basic functions and 8,099 points for productivity show that web browsers, Word, and spreadsheets run smoothly. For digital content creation, the score drops to 5,130 points. Programs launch quickly, but running several large applications pushes the 8 GB of LPDDR5 RAM to its limits. Unfortunately, the RAM is soldered in place and cannot be upgraded. Anyone using lots of browser tabs, Microsoft Teams, and image-editing software simultaneously should expect short delays. Christoph Hoffmann The 3DMark CPU Profile confirms the unbalanced core configuration. A single thread scores 1,027 points, while two threads reach 1,615 points. With four threads, the score is 2,691 points and the maximum score is 3,331 points. The single P-core responds quickly, but during prolonged rendering or video conversion, additional powerful cores are needed. The UniBook is best suited for Office tasks, research, and media playback. Software development, large RAW projects, and video rendering require more patience. Christoph Hoffmann The integrated Intel graphics uses just one Xe3 core running at up to 2.3 GHz. Its performance is sufficient for navigating Windows’ interface and video playback. In 3DMark Time Spy, the UniBook scores 893 points, although 3DMark flags the result with a warning. The graphics score is 783 points, while the CPU score is 4,383 points. Despite the lack of validation, the result suggests that the graphics performance is likely sufficient only for older or less demanding games. Christoph Hoffmann Demanding games run too slowly, even at 1080p. Newer 3DMark tests wouldn’t run because the graphics unit lacks hardware ray tracing and other DirectX 12 Ultimate features. According to the manufacturer, the NPU achieves 15 TOPS. This is sufficient for individual local AI functions, but does not meet the requirements of a Copilot Plus PC. The 256 GB HOGE H750 NVMe SSD uses PCIe 3.0. CrystalDiskMark records sequential read speeds of 2,383 MB/s and write speeds of 2,101 MB/s. That’s respectable for a budget laptop. Around 237 GB is available after formatting, though Windows reduces the available space further. The M.2-2280 SSD can be swapped for a larger PCIe 3.0 or PCIe 4.0 model. A second SSD cannot be installed. Christoph Hoffmann The MSI Modern 15’s Ryzen 5 7530U processor offers six cores and twelve threads. It performs noticeably faster on parallelized tasks and features more powerful Radeon graphics. Its RAM is also not upgradeable. The UniBook, on the other hand, is more compact, lighter, and has longer battery life. If you prioritize value above all else, you’re better off with an affordable Ryzen 5 model. For commuters, the Chuwi offers a good balance between size, battery life, and connectivity options. Chuwi UniBook: Battery life The built-in lithium-polymer battery has a capacity of 53.38 Wh. In our battery test, with the display brightness set to 150 cd/m², the UniBook lasted around 13 hours and 40 minutes. At maximum brightness, the battery life drops to just under twelve hours. This is more than enough for a working day involving word processing, web browsing, and short video conferences. In idle mode, we measured power consumption of around 2.5 to 4.8 watts, depending on the display brightness. Under typical load, consumption rises to around 18 watts. For short periods, it can reach just over 50 watts. The included 65-watt power adaptor has plenty of headroom and can charge via either of the two USB-C ports. A charge level of around 60 percent can be reached after about an hour. The manufacturer’s claim of up to 20 hours, however, depends heavily on light use and low display brightness. In everyday use, 12 to 14 hours is more realistic. Chuwi UniBook: Cooling, noise level The UniBook actively cools the Core 3 304 with a single fan. When idle or during light office work, the fan often stops running. As a result, the notebook operates silently. Short periods of heavy processing usually result in only a faint hum. Under full load, the noise level briefly rises to over 40 dB(A), but drops to around 30 dB(A) after the initial power surge. Compared to the MSI Modern 15, the cooling system seems more restrained, as the MSI fan is clearly audible under load. The processor briefly draws up to 35 watts at the start of a task, allowing programs to launch quickly. After a few seconds, the firmware reduces power consumption to 15 watts to keep the laptop cool and quiet. As a result, computing performance drops during longer tasks such as rendering. Christoph Hoffmann Even under load, the chassis only warms up moderately. Using the Thermal Master 3 thermal imaging camera, we measured a maximum of 101.5 degrees on the top surface. The warmest area is above the keyboard near the hinge. The keys and the palm rest remain significantly cooler. On the underside, the UniBook reaches a maximum of 90.9 degrees. This means it’s pretty comfortable to use on your lap. Just make sure the ventilation slots aren’t blocked. Chuwi has sensibly tailored the cooling system to its target audience. The UniBook causes no disturbance, especially in a quiet working environment. The trade-off is not thermal throttling in the problematic sense, but rather a fixed performance budget. This configuration is well-suited to office software. Users with constant CPU loads will benefit more from a laptop with multiple performance cores and a larger cooler. Chuwi UniBook: Conclusion The Chuwi UniBook impresses in situations where an affordable device needs to be practical. The metal casing is lightweight and well-finished. The keyboard is suitable for longer typing sessions, and the battery lasts a full working day. Five USB ports, HDMI, a card reader, and Gigabit LAN mean many users won’t need an adapter. For $449, this combination is rare. The cost-cutting measures remain evident. The display is matte and sharp, but covers only around 59 percent of the sRGB color space. Colors appear correspondingly pale. The webcam and speakers deliver basic quality. A more significant drawback is the 8 GB of soldered-on RAM. Even with demanding multitasking, there’s little room to maneuver. The Core 3 304 offers good responsiveness per core, but it doesn’t match the Ryzen 5’s performance under sustained load. Its modest Xe3 graphics are hardly suitable for gaming. Anyone looking for a quiet, long-lasting laptop for office work will find this a well-rounded package. Buyers should assess their storage requirements and not expect any spare capacity for resource-intensive creative software. The MSI Modern 15 is larger and heavier, but offers more processing and graphics performance with the Ryzen 5 7530U. The UniBook wins when it comes to portability, but not when it comes to performance. Chuwi UniBook: Specs Processor: Intel Core 3 304, Wildcat Lake, 1 P-core plus 4 LP-E cores, 5 threads, up to 4.3 GHz, 6 MB L3 cache, 15 watts Graphics: Intel Graphics, 1 Xe3 core, up to 2.3 GHz, 9 TOPS NPU: Intel NPU 5, up to 15 TOPS RAM: 8 GB LPDDR5-6400, soldered, dual-channel Storage: 256 GB HOGE H750 NVMe SSD, PCIe 3.0, M.2 2280, removable; slot supports PCIe 4.0 x4 Display: 14-inch, IPS, matt, 1,920 × 1,200 pixels, 16:10, 60 Hz Ports on the left: 2 × USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 with charging and DisplayPort, HDMI 1.4b, USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 Ports on the right: USB-A 3.2 Gen 1, USB-A 2.0, Gigabit Ethernet, micro SD card reader, 3.5 mm audio Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6 via Realtek RTL8852BE, Bluetooth 5.2 Camera: 720p with mechanical privacy cover Keyboard: Chiclet, two-level white backlighting, QWERTY layout on the test unit Audio: Stereo speakers, combined headphone/microphone jack Battery: 53.38 Wh lithium-polymer Power adaptor: 65 watts, USB-C Power Delivery Dimensions: 314.5 × 221 × 16.4 mm Weight: approx. 1.2 kg Warranty: 12 months Operating system: Windows 11 Pro Software: Office Professional Plus 2024
